options.text: Across the cell membrane by diffusion, osmosis and active transport
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
They have no vessels.

questions.stem: What geometric property lets a single cell rely on diffusion?

options.explanation: Thick membranes lengthen diffusion paths.

options.text: A large surface area relative to its volume
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: A small surface area to save energy
options.explanation: Small surface would slow exchange.

options.text: A spherical shape of maximum volume
options.explanation: Volume is the problem, not the goal.

options.explanation: Amoeba is not photosynthetic.

options.text: Its surface-to-centre distance is so short that membrane diffusion meets its needs

questions.stem: State why unicellular organisms can rely on diffusion alone.
questions.modelAnswer: Their large surface area relative to volume keeps diffusion distances short, so membrane exchange meets all their needs.

questions.stem: Name the organism used as the single-celled example here.
questions.modelAnswer: The amoeba exchanges oxygen inward and carbon dioxide outward across its membrane.

questions.stem: Explain why diffusion distance matters so much to a single cell.
questions.modelAnswer: Because diffusion slows steeply with distance, and a short surface-to-centre path lets gases and wastes move fast enough to service the whole cell volume.

questions.stem: A single-celled organism grows to ten times its diameter. Predict its exchange problem.
questions.modelAnswer: Its volume rises far faster than its surface area, so the interior sits far from the membrane, and diffusion alone can no longer supply the core.

questions.stem: Why can multicellular organisms not rely on diffusion alone?

options.explanation: Every cell has a membrane.

options.text: Their many cell layers make diffusion distances too long for adequate speed
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because their skin blocks all diffusion
options.explanation: Skin is one layer; depth is the real issue.
Temperature is irrelevant to this argument.

questions.stem: Which system transports substances in animals?

options.explanation: Lymph drains fluid; blood does the hauling.

options.text: The circulatory system, carrying them in the blood

options.explanation: Chlorophyll stays in the chloroplasts.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: State the transport systems of animals and plants.
questions.modelAnswer: Animals use the circulatory system in the blood; plants use the vascular system of xylem and phloem.

questions.stem: Name the two jobs of the plant vascular system.
questions.modelAnswer: Xylem hauls water and minerals up from the roots, while phloem distributes sugars and amino acids.

questions.stem: Explain why being many cells thick creates a transport need.
questions.modelAnswer: Because each extra layer lengthens the diffusion path from the surface, and past a few layers the centre cannot be supplied quickly enough by diffusion alone.

questions.stem: An flatworm is thin and flat; a roundworm is cylindrical. Which needs more transport provision and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The cylindrical worm: its greater thickness puts interior cells farther from the surface, so diffusion alone struggles where the flatworm's short paths suffice.
